summary: After core functions in OpenAI’s FedRAMP workspaces had returned, six functions remained unavailable. In a 29 June 2026 update, OpenAI named Codex, workspace analytics, conversation search, search for custom GPTs, ChatGPT user invitations and the Compliance Logs Platform download endpoint as still not working. It said it was investigating and working to resolve them. OpenAI marked the broader incident resolved at 2:11 a.m. on 11 July, saying core functionality was restored. The notice does not state when the wider interruption first began or whether the underlying compliance logs were lost.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Full taxonomy 0.6.7 review retains unclassified status. FC-000044 Primary Evidence Accessibility requires an authoritative artefact, authorised reviewer, material review question and blocked direct inspection in that context; an unavailable download endpoint alone does not prove those conditions. FC-000024 Audit-Trail Reconstructability requires inadequate logs for reconstructing a material event, not merely a temporarily unavailable retrieval endpoint. FC-000037 Control Availability Determination requires an uncertainty about a defined control before a decision. No such additional occurrence facts are established.

classification_review_provenance.authority_boundary: FC-000044, FC-000024 and FC-000037 tested; none accepted. Compliance-log endpoint interruption is observed, but reviewer, artefact, review question and loss of log integrity are not. No compliance breach inferred.

assessment_boundaries: The first preserved update describes residual problems after core functionality returned, not the onset of the broader incident.
The notice does not show whether compliance logs were collected, retained, available by another route or needed for a particular audit.
The provider did not publish root cause, affected customer count or continuous per-feature duration in the accessible notice.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: OpenAI’s 29 June update says core FedRAMP workspace functionality had returned while Codex, analytics, conversation search, custom GPT search, invitations and the Compliance Logs Platform download endpoint remained nonfunctional. Its 11 July update declares the broader incident resolved. Those two dated updates establish that the named residual problems were publicly acknowledged across nearly twelve calendar days; the third-party mirror measures a narrower 1–11 July window. The notice does not establish the initial outage time, that every feature was continuously down for the whole interval, whether compliance logs themselves were retained, whether another access route existed, or that a named reviewer missed a material audit. The provider statement identifies a download endpoint failure, not loss of underlying audit records.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The provider identified six unavailable FedRAMP workspace functions after core service returned and later declared resolution. The failed compliance-log download route warrants governance attention because it is a route to audit material. Yet the report does not identify an authoritative log artefact needed by an authorised reviewer for a material question, show that equivalent access was unavailable, or show a reconstruction failure. The occurrence therefore supports operational impairment and a specific potential evidence-access boundary, but remains unclassified rather than assigning a failure class from the endpoint name alone.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The residual defects included collaboration and discovery functions, but also a compliance-log download route that could be relevant to oversight. The status notice makes the endpoint’s unavailability visible while leaving open the fate of the logs, alternate retrieval routes and any concrete review it interrupted. Those are the decisive facts for assessing an evidence-access governance failure.
